transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone thanks for joining, appreciate you all making time. Quick intros - I'm Maya, AE on the account, and with me is Diego from our infra/security team.
[00:12] Diego (Redwood SE): Hi, Diego Ramos, platform/infra, I'll be the deep dive person on networking and private deployments.
[00:18] Eleanor (Seacliff): Eleanor here, Head of Cloud. We run most workloads in us-east-1 and a second DR region in eu-west-1. Marcus is our security lead, Sharon's our CTO.
[00:28] Sharon (Seacliff): Hi all.
[00:30] Maya: Great. Objective today is to understand your VPC/topology constraints and whether Redwood Private (VPC deployment) fits - peering vs endpoints, region constraints, KMS, etc.
[00:42] Marcus: Cool, high-level we have strict egress controls, all outbound traffic goes through a set of proxy NAT instances and then through a transit gateway. We also have cross-account peering for partner workloads. We need to know what networking footprint Redwood would require.
[00:58] Diego: Totally. At a high level our Private option can run in your VPC (customer-managed) or in a customer-dedicated VPC we manage with peering/private endpoints - two common patterns. If you want zero egress through public internet, we can do AWS interface endpoints (PrivateLink) or set up cross-account VPC peering plus route table entries.
[01:20] Eleanor: We prefer not to expose any endpoints to the public internet. Interface endpoints are OK but our security team prefers VPC peering because we can control security groups and flow logs centrally.
[01:33] Diego: Understood. A couple things to watch for with peering: overlapping CIDR blocks, route table limits, and the fact peering doesn't support transitive routing - so if you use a transit gateway it's often cleaner. Does Seacliff use a transit gateway?
[01:47] Marcus: Yes, we have a TGW for cross-account traffic. We also use specific route table blacklists for certain subnets.
[01:55] Maya: Good to know. If we bring Redwood into your account as customer-managed our recommend pattern is deploying a dedicated subnet group, then we can attach an ENI or set up a PrivateLink endpoint in your account. For TGW customers, we usually ask for a peering attachment to the TGW or a managed VPC that peers to your TGW.
[02:10] Sharon: Quick question - what ports and protocols do you need?
[02:14] Diego: Typically HTTPS (443) for control plane communications, and gRPC/HTTPS for the inference traffic depending on model routing. We can also speak over private TLS endpoints, nothing raw. The security groups will be narrow: control plane to specific IPs or endpoint DNS names.
[02:28] Marcus: And how about egress? Our proxy forces outbound through our egress proxies, we don't allow instances to talk direct outbound. Would Redwood need direct internet?
[02:39] Diego: We can support flows through your NAT/proxy. Two patterns: 1) customer-managed VPC where the Redwood services sit inside your private subnets and egress via your proxy; 2) Redwood-managed VPC with inter-VPC peering and we route through your TGW. If you need to force all outbound through your proxies we can configure the deployment so outgoing calls (updates, telemetry, container images) go through your proxy or S3 endpoints.
[03:02] Eleanor: That aligns. We also want control over KMS keys. We can't have Redwood hold keys. Is bring-your-own-KMS supported?
[03:11] Maya: Yes, BYO-KMS is supported for data-at-rest. We integrate with customer-managed KMS keys via IAM roles and key policies. For HSM-backed keys, we have a connector flow but that will need a deeper security review.
[03:23] Marcus: Ok good. We also need audit logs forwarded to our SIEM and retain logs for seven years per policy.
[03:29] Diego: We ship audit logs and access logs and can forward them to your CloudWatch/Stackdriver or S3 bucket via cross-account role. We can also push to your Splunk/Elastic via subscription. There was a slight hiccup in one customer's flow where the automated log-forwarder needed explicit bucket policies, so we'll include that in the doc.
[03:45] Sharon: What about region constraints - we need our production model serving in us-east-1 for latency but DR in eu-west-1. Can Redwood replicate across regions?
[03:54] Maya: Yes, Redwood supports multi-region deployments. For Private, we can set up a primary cluster in us-east-1 and a standby in eu-west-1. Cross-region replication of model artifacts and KV cache is supported, but note that KV cache warmup and cold-start latency differ. We recommend async replication for artifacts and a warm-up plan for keys.
[04:12] Marcus: Would traffic failover be automatic?
[04:15] Diego: We support routing policies - health-check based failover via DNS with low TTLs or route through your global load balancer. For strict RTOs we recommend active-active in both regions, but that doubles resource footprint. We'll outline tradeoffs.
[04:31] Eleanor: How do you handle private image pulls (ECR) in our account?
[04:35] Diego: If we're deploying into your account, we can use your ECR repositories and an IAM role to pull images. If we manage the cluster, we request read-only access to your ECR or use a cross-account role.
[04:46] Maya: Also call out that for dedicated GPU instances there are AMIs and kernel modules we install; sometimes corporate hardened AMIs block some kernel features - we'll run a compatibility checklist.
[04:58] Marcus: About peering - we have overlapping ranges with one of our partners which complicates peering. Is PrivateLink better in that case?
[05:06] Diego: Yes, PrivateLink avoids CIDR overlap because it's an interface endpoint; it's effectively a set of ENIs in your subnets, and we talk to that endpoint using private DNS. But PrivateLink has throughput/cost characteristics; for high throughput inference workloads peering+TGW might be more economical. We'll include numbers.
[05:26] Eleanor: Throughput - we're expecting bursts up to 30k tokens/sec for batch jobs and sustained real-time traffic of about 800 requests per second. What does that mean for peering vs PrivateLink?
[05:36] Diego: For sustained high RPS, peering with a TGW and dedicated ENIs is usually better. PrivateLink has per-GB charges and might increase latency slightly, though usually negligible. We'll give a cost/latency table for your expected profile.
[05:49] Sharon: What about our compliance needs - SOC 2 and ISO are must-haves. Are you SOC 2 certified and can we get the report?
[05:57] Maya: Redwood is SOC 2 Type II and we can share attestation under an NDA. For Private deployments we also provide guidance to map our controls to your audit requirements. We'll include the security pack in the next email.
[06:10] Marcus: Network logging - we require VPC flow logs plus RBAC on service accounts.
[06:15] Diego: We support flow logs from our ENIs or you can enable flow logs in your account and we can pull them. For RBAC, our operator integrates with your IAM and supports SAML & OIDC for user access.
[06:26] Eleanor: Any special DNS requirements? We run an internal Resolver and split-horizon DNS.
[06:31] Diego: We can support private DNS with PrivateLink and route 53 inbound endpoints. In split-horizon setups we sometimes need to add conditional forwarding or private hosted zones in your account. We'll document the recommended DNS topology.
[06:46] Maya: Quick note on upgrades: we do rolling upgrades and support canary deploys. If you run strict change control, we can tie upgrades to your change window and ship a canary first.
[06:58] Sharon: On billing and metering if you're in our VPC how do we meter usage?
[07:03] Maya: We provide token-level metrics and billing reports. For Private deployments billing can be invoiced via contract (monthly) and we can instrument per-route token counts exported to your monitoring if needed.
[07:16] Marcus: On the connectivity side, do you need public IPs for the control plane?
[07:20] Diego: Our control plane usually talks to the deployment for management. For strictly air-gapped requirements we offer an offline bundle or a fully private control plane inside your VPC, but that requires extra integration work. If your policy forbids all public egress, we'll plan for a customer-managed control plane.
[07:36] Eleanor: Good to confirm. We're not fully air-gapped but we want no public ingress - only private endpoints.
[07:43] Diego: That's fine. We'll ensure endpoints are interface endpoints and tightened security groups.
[07:48] Maya: Quick follow: what's your timeline and success criteria?
[07:52] Sharon: Timeline Q3 pilot - want an internal POC by mid-July; success criteria: under 100ms 95th percentile latency for common prompts in us-east-1, no traffic leaving our VPC for inference requests, and KMS keys under our control.
[08:08] Maya: Perfect, that's actionable. We'll package the POC plan.
[08:12] Marcus: A couple of gotchas - our TGW enforces route propagation restrictions and we expect strict subnet tagging policies. Also any cross-account role must be approved by our security team.
[08:23] Diego: We can provide a least-privilege IAM role template and a terraform module to create the necessary infra with tags. That tends to speed approvals.
[08:34] Eleanor: On the model side, can we pin a specific version? We need deterministic outputs for a financial workflow.
[08:41] Maya: Yes, version pinning and rollbacks are supported. We'll also surface model-card info and evaluation results. If you need model explainability telemetry we'll discuss offline.
[08:53] Marcus: Any specifics about latency determinism - GPU cold starts, kv cache warmup?
[08:58] Diego: Cold starts happen when the KV cache or model weights aren't resident. For inference serving we keep active models warm; during POC we can provision reserved capacity to avoid cold starts. KV cache warmup is dependent on your prompt distribution - we can pre-seed caches with replay data for the POC.
[09:17] Maya: Also we have a feature for prefix caching which can dramatically improve latency if you have repeated prefixes. That might be relevant for templated financial prompts.
[09:26] Sharon: Let's talk SSO/roles for our devs to access the console - must be SAML.
[09:31] Diego: SAML SSO is supported; we can map roles to your groups and support SCIM provisioning for user sync.
[09:39] Maya: We're about 10 minutes in - wanted to leave time for network specifics. Marcus can you share your VPC CIDRs and TGW attachments?
[09:47] Marcus: Sure, I'll send. We have 10.10.0.0/16, 10.20.0.0/16 and partner VPCs that use 172.16.0.0/16 - it's the overlap with partner VPCs that complicates peering.
[09:58] Diego: Okay that explains the PrivateLink preference. We'll draft two patterns in the doc: 1) PrivateLink + endpoint service (recommended for CIDR overlap but with cost considerations); 2) TGW peering with dedicated subnets if you can route.
[10:11] Eleanor: For PrivateLink what's the experience for DNS?
[10:14] Diego: We publish a private DNS name that resolves to the interface endpoint. You can override with private hosted zones. We also support mTLS if you want mutual TLS between your clients and endpoint.
[10:25] Marcus: mTLS would be preferred.
[10:27] Diego: We can support mTLS; we'll need your CA chain and cert provisioning process.
[10:34] Maya: Do you have any corporate firewalls that do SNI inspection or TLS interception?
[10:38] Marcus: Yes, we have a proxy that does TLS inspection for egress. We need to check whether it will break mTLS.
[10:45] Diego: If TLS is intercepted then mTLS will fail - we'll coordinate with your proxy team. There are patterns where we offload certification at the endpoint and use internal auth tokens - we'll outline options.
[10:58] Sharon: About data retention: our data cannot leave account and must be purged after 30 days unless archived.
[11:05] Maya: We can configure retention and have TTLs for logs/model artifacts. For data that must not leave the account, the customer-managed VPC option is the cleanest; all storage stays in your account.
[11:18] Eleanor: One more question on routing: in our setup you said peering isn't transitive; with TGW is there any additional configuration to allow traffic from on-prem to reach Redwood?
[11:27] Diego: If you have VPN/Direct Connect attached to TGW, we can accept route propagation and ensure security groups allow on-prem subnets. We'll ask for the list of on-prem CIDRs.
[11:37] Marcus: We'll include those.
[11:39] Maya: Okay timeline recap: We will send an architecture doc with two network patterns (PrivateLink and TGW peering), include IAM/role templates, a compatibility checklist for AMIs and kernel features, and the SOC 2 pack. Diego will do the VPC compatibility check after we get CIDRs and TGW details.
[11:56] Diego: One more note on metrics - we can push per-token latency histograms and traces into your observability if you give us a metrics endpoint or a read-only ingestion role.
[12:06] Eleanor: We'll want that for the POC.
[12:08] Maya: Perfect. Any blocking items?
[12:11] Sharon: No blockers - need to review the doc and then we'll schedule the security deep dive.
[12:15] Maya: Great. I'll follow up with an email and the doc early next week. Thanks everyone.
[12:20] Speaker 1: (inaudible)
[12:22] Maya: Ending call.

Notes: Transcription has some minor mis-words (K V cash -> KV cache, etc.). References to shared artifacts: link: /redwood/private-deploy-arch-v1.pdf (will be attached in follow-up).
